title: Mars 2020 Perseverance: Entry, Descent and Landing (EDL)

site.name: Octavia E. Butler Landing, Jezero Crater

light_time_note: One-way light time on landing day: 11 min 22 s (press kit). Radio travelled ≈204 million km, so Earth learned of every event 11 min 22 s after it happened.
clock_note: Entry interface spacecraft event time ≈20:36:39 UTC, derived from touchdown received at Earth ≈20:55 UTC minus 11 min 22 s light time minus E+6:59. Press releases round to the minute.

events.label: Cruise stage separation
events.text: The ring-shaped cruise stage, with its solar panels and radiators, has carried the rover for six and a half months. Ten minutes before the atmosphere it is cut loose. From now on the aeroshell flies alone.

events.label: Cruise balance masses ejected
events.text: Two 75 kg tungsten blocks are thrown overboard. Losing them shifts the centre of mass off the symmetry axis, so the capsule will fly tilted at about 16° — and a tilted capsule makes lift, which it can steer.

events.label: Entry interface
events.text: The top of the atmosphere, defined as 3,522.2 km from the centre of Mars. The capsule arrives at about 19,500 km/h, angled 15.5° below the horizon. Get the angle wrong by a degree and it either skips off or plunges too deep.

events.label: Guided entry begins
events.text: Once drag reaches 0.2 Earth g the computer starts steering. It cannot point the lift where it likes — it rolls the whole capsule (the bank angle). Lift pointed up stretches the flight; lift pointed down shortens it.

events.label: Peak heating
events.text: The gas in front of the heat shield is squeezed so hard it becomes a glowing plasma. The PICA heat shield (Phenolic Impregnated Carbon Ablator) chars and slowly burns away, carrying heat off with it.

events.label: Bank reversal 1
events.text: Banking pushes the capsule sideways as well as down. To keep drifting sideways under control, the computer rolls to the opposite bank angle — a bank reversal. Perseverance made three.

events.label: Peak deceleration
events.text: The heaviest braking: about ten times Earth's gravity. The rover, which weighs 3.8 kN on Mars, briefly weighs as much as 100 kN. Peak dynamic pressure is about 15 kPa.

events.label: Bank reversal 2
events.text: Second roll reversal. The corridor for sideways error narrows as the capsule slows, so reversals come closer together.

events.label: Bank reversal 3
events.text: Third and last reversal.

events.label: Heading alignment
events.text: Below 1,100 m/s the guidance stops worrying about range and uses small bank angles (at most 30°) to point straight at the target.

events.label: Straighten Up and Fly Right (SUFR)
events.text: Six 25 kg tungsten entry balance masses are ejected. The centre of mass moves back onto the axis, the capsule flies straight (no lift) and the rolling stops, so the parachute opens cleanly.

events.label: Parachute deploy (Range Trigger)
events.text: A mortar fires the packed 21.5 m supersonic disk-gap-band parachute out at about 140 km/h (39 m/s on Curiosity). The Range Trigger opens it when the capsule reaches the planned point over the ground, not at a fixed speed, which halves the downrange error. Peak inflation load was about 152 kN (34,200 lbf).

events.label: Heat shield separation
events.text: The heat shield drops away, uncovering the rover and the descent stage for the first time. The radar and the Lander Vision System (LVS) cameras can now see the ground.

events.label: Lander Vision System starts
events.text: A downward camera takes pictures and matches landmarks against an onboard map made from orbit. This is Terrain-Relative Navigation (TRN), used on Mars for the first time.

events.label: TRN fix and safe target chosen
events.text: Knowing where it really is (to about 40 m), the spacecraft looks up the safest reachable spot in its hazard map and plans a divert to it. Without TRN, Jezero's cliffs, boulder fields and dunes were too risky.

events.label: Backshell separation
events.text: The descent stage and rover drop out of the backshell, leaving the parachute behind.

events.label: Powered descent
events.text: Eight throttleable hydrazine rockets light up. First they steer away from the falling backshell and parachute, then they fly to the safe target.

events.label: Divert to the safe target
events.text: The divert is flown open-eyed: the vehicle knows its position from TRN and its height and speed from radar.

events.label: Constant-velocity descent
events.text: Near 20 m the descent slows to a steady 0.75 m/s straight down, the speed the rover will touch down at.

events.label: Sky crane
events.text: Nylon bridles spool out and lower the rover 7.6 m (25 ft) below the hovering descent stage. On the way down the rover unfolds its wheels.

events.label: Bridles fully out
events.text: The rover hangs on its bridles like a pendulum. The descent stage keeps sinking at 0.75 m/s.

events.label: Touchdown
events.text: The wheels take the weight. The descent stage feels the thrust it needs drop, and that is how it knows it has landed.

events.label: Bridles cut
events.text: Pyrotechnic cutters sever the bridles and the umbilical.

events.label: Descent stage flyaway
events.text: The descent stage throttles up, climbs, tilts away and flies off to crash a safe distance from the rover.

events.label: Descent stage impact
events.text: The descent stage hits the ground roughly 700 m away. Its job is done.
